title: Why is Integer 100 == 100 true but Integer 1000 == 1000 false?
shortTitle: Why is Integer 100 == 100 true but Integer 1000 == 1000 false?
keyPoints: Integer.valueOf() caches objects for -128 to 127 – two Integers in range share the same object
== on objects compares references (identity), not values – it accidentally works inside the cache
Outside the cache, valueOf() creates new objects each time – == returns false even for equal values
.equals() compares the actual int values and always returns the correct answer
The cache upper bound is tunable via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax or -Djava.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high
Same trap exists for Long (-128 to 127), but Float and Double are never cached

s1_definition.oneliner: Integer.valueOf() caches objects for -128 to 127. Inside the cache, == returns true because both references point to the same shared object. Outside, == returns false because each call creates a new object. Use .equals() to compare values.
s1_definition.profdef:
The behavior comes from three facts:

- **Autoboxing calls valueOf().** Writing `Integer a = 100` compiles to `Integer a = Integer.valueOf(100)`.
- **valueOf() caches -128 to 127.** For values in this range, it returns the same pre-created object every time. For values outside, it creates a new object.
- **== compares references, not values.** Two references to the same cached object compare as equal. Two different objects with the same value compare as not equal.

The fix is simple: always use `.equals()` or unbox to primitives.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank keeps a tray of 256 pre-printed token cards numbered -128 to 127. When two customers ask for token 100, the clerk hands out the same card from the tray. Holding them side by side, they are the same physical card, so asking "is this the identical card?" (==) says yes. For token 1000, no pre-printed card exists. The clerk prints a fresh one each time. Now two cards say 1000 but they are different pieces of paper, so "is this the identical card?" says no. Asking "do both cards show the same amount?" (.equals()) always gives the right answer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Integer a = 100           Integer a = 1000
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  Integer.valueOf(100)      Integer.valueOf(1000)
       │                         │
  in cache? YES             in cache? NO
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  return cache[228]         return new Integer(1000)
       │                         │
  Integer b = 100           Integer b = 1000
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  Integer.valueOf(100)      Integer.valueOf(1000)
       │                         │
  return cache[228]         return new Integer(1000)
  (SAME object)             (DIFFERENT object)
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  a == b → TRUE             a == b → FALSE
  (same reference)          (different references)
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  a.equals(b) → TRUE        a.equals(b) → TRUE
  (value comparison)         (value comparison)


  Cache boundary:
    -128  ........................  127  |  128 ..... 1000 ..... MAX
    ◀─────── cached (== works) ─────────▶  ◀── not cached (== fails) ──▶


  Wrapper cache summary:
    Integer:   -128 to 127 (tunable upper)     Float:     never
    Long:      -128 to 127 (fixed)             Double:    never
    Short:     -128 to 127 (fixed)             Boolean:   always (2 values)
    Byte:      -128 to 127 (full range)        Character: 0 to 127
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason Integer 100 compared with == returns true but Integer 1000 returns false is the Integer cache inside `valueOf()`. When you write `Integer a = 100`, the compiler calls `Integer.valueOf(100)`, which returns a pre-created shared object from a cache that covers -128 to 127. Both `a` and `b` receive the same object, so `==` (which compares references) returns true.

For 1000, which is outside the cache, `valueOf` creates a new Integer object each time. The two references point to different objects, so `==` returns false even though the values are identical. This is not a bug in Java. It is the expected behavior of reference comparison on objects. The bug is in the code that uses `==` instead of `.equals()`.

The fix is simple. Always compare wrapper objects with `.equals()`, which compares the underlying int values. Or unbox to primitives and compare with `==`, which compares values directly. If either side might be null, use `Objects.equals()` for null safety.

The same trap exists for `Long`, `Short`, and `Character` (all cache -128 to 127). `Byte` is always cached because its entire range fits. `Float` and `Double` are never cached, so `==` on them always compares references.

One sentence to remember: `==` on Integer compares object identity and only accidentally works inside the -128 to 127 cache; always use `.equals()` to compare values.
